"Now, within this assembly, there is a gathering of immeasurable śrāvakas and bodhisattvas who are capable of being instructed.
At that time, after Upāli had spoken these words, the Buddha said to Upāli:

"For the sake of the śrāvakas, you should provide specific instructions on pure conduct according to their capacities; furthermore, for the sake of bodhisattvas who have newly begun practicing the Mahāyāna, you should skillfully employ expedient means to provide specific instructions on pure conduct according to their capacities."
Why is this so? Upāli!

If a śrāvaka upholds the precepts, you should know that the distinctions in their practice of those precepts are contrary to the bodhisattva precepts first cultivated by a Mahāyāna bodhisattva; therefore, they do not constitute the pure precepts of a bodhisattva.

If a Bodhisattva who has newly begun the Mahāyāna maintains pure precepts, these would then be contrary to and different from the ascetic practices of the Śrāvakas, and thus would not constitute pure precepts. Why is this so?

If, by the power of their resolve, Śrāvakas do not seek even for a single moment the cycle of birth and death in the world, nor take pleasure in it, nor aspire to it—this is the pure conduct of the precepts of those Śrāvakas.
If a bodhisattva who has first begun practicing the Mahāyāna, by the power of their vow and aspiration, thinks:
"May I, throughout immeasurable eons, rescue and deliver sentient beings from this ocean of suffering, my mind never weary."
"This is the pure practice of the precepts for bodhisattvas who have first begun to cultivate Mahāyāna practices.
For this reason, Upāli, you should know that the prohibitions and precepts must each be taught according to the individual's capacity."
"If one speaks of precepts for a bodhisattva newly cultivating Mahāyāna practices, they accord with the minds of others and do not afflict sentient beings;
if one speaks of precepts for a śrāvaka, they are for the benefit of oneself and do not accord with the minds of others."
If for the sake of bodhisattvas newly cultivating the Mahāyāna, one teaches precepts that are lenient and skillful in means;
if for the sake of śrāvakas, one teaches precepts that allow no leniency, with prohibitions that are strict and urgent.
If for the sake of bodhisattvas who are beginners in the Mahāyāna, one speaks of precepts that can endure for a long time, these are spoken from the perspective of signlessness;
if for the sake of śrāvakas, one speaks of precepts that can be strict and severe, these are spoken from the perspective of grasping at signs.
“Upāli! For what reason are bodhisattvas who first practice the Mahāyāna path instructed to train while also complying with the intentions of others?
And for what reason are śrāvakas instructed to train without complying with the intentions of others?”
Upāli, you should know this:

Bodhisattvas who first cultivate the practices of the Mahāyāna each guide and transform sentient beings according to their individual capacities; they cultivate the practice of the precepts because they accord with the minds of others and because they cause no affliction to others.
If it is a Śrāvaka, however, he cultivates the practice of the precepts not for the sake of the minds of others.
"Why is it that the bodhisattva who first practices the Mahāyāna path has broad and tolerant precepts with no transgressions,
whereas the prohibitions of the śrāvakas are narrow and strict?
Upāli, you should know this:"

If a bodhisattva newly practicing the Mahāyāna commits an offense in the early morning, they should acknowledge the transgression; however, if by midday their bodhicitta remains uninterrupted, the aggregate of precepts is perfected and it is not considered an offense.
If they commit an offense at midday, but by evening their bodhicitta remains uninterrupted, the accumulation of precepts is perfected and it is not considered an offense.
If they commit an offense in the evening, but by the first watch of night their bodhicitta remains uninterrupted, the accumulation of precepts is perfected and it is not considered an offense.

If there is an offense during the first watch of the night, provided that the bodhicitta remains uninterrupted until the middle watch and the accumulation of precepts is perfected, it does not constitute an offense;

if there is an offense during the middle watch, provided that the bodhicitta remains uninterrupted until the final watch and the accumulation of precepts is perfected, it does not constitute an offense.
Upāli, you should know this:
when a bodhisattva first practices the Mahāyāna path, their bodhisattva precepts are broad and lenient; if a bodhisattva incurs an offense or transgression, they should not feel regret or fear.
Furthermore, if a śrāvaka violates the precepts, the characteristics of their morality are extinguished and can never be restored in their entirety. Why is this?

Because when a śrāvaka upholds the precepts to eliminate afflictions, they act as if their head were on fire or their robes were ablaze, swiftly seeking the tranquility of nirvāṇa and firmly maintaining their ascetic conduct.
"How is it that a bodhisattva who has first set out on the Mahāyāna path practices for a long time without signs and without attachment, yet does not depart from the world?
How is it that a śrāvaka clings to signs, seeking to sever and extinguish [defilements] in a single lifetime, practicing and training in what is manifest before him?"

Upāli! If a bodhisattva who has first begun practicing the Mahāyāna path were to experience the pleasures of the five desires for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, yet never for a moment abandon the bodhicitta, you should know that this bodhisattva’s observance of the precepts is without flaw.

Why is this? It is because for a bodhisattva who has first begun practicing the Mahāyāna path, the bodhicitta will later reach maturity; even while asleep, they remain unstained by the five desires, let alone while awake.

Why is this? A bodhisattva who has newly begun practicing the Mahāyāna path should not completely sever all afflictions in a single lifetime; rather, when their bodhi matures, the afflictions will naturally cease.

If the śrāvakas have not yet matured in their cultivation of the path, their minds do not wish to be born again in the world for even a single kṣaṇa; therefore, they practice with such rapidity throughout a single lifetime as one who seeks to extinguish a fire on their head.
Upāli, you should know this:
a bodhisattva who first practices the Mahāyāna path does so for a long duration, entering into practice with a mind free from weariness;
one should know that a śrāvaka practices and studies for only a single lifetime and for a brief period.

For this reason, Upāli! If you are to instruct a bodhisattva who is a beginner in the Mahāyāna practice regarding the precepts, you should teach them with broad scope and flexibility in order to accommodate the inclinations of others; you must instruct them in a manner that is far-reaching and profound, leading them to cultivate and study these teachings.
If one teaches the precepts for the sake of śrāvakas, one should not comply with others' whims, nor should there be any laxity. Why is this?

A bodhisattva who first practices the Mahāyāna path cultivates the vessel of the Dharma through great causes and conditions in order to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; such a bodhisattva should not feel weary of or afraid of the world.
"I vow that for immeasurable and long eons, I shall undergo the suffering of birth and death for the sake of sentient beings.

For this reason, the Tathāgata did not speak of the causes and conditions for repentance as a means of escaping the ocean of birth and death within the triple world for the sake of practicing bodhisattvas.

Why is this? Because the Tathāgata, out of joy and a heart of gladness for the sake of the practicing bodhisattva, speaks of the profound, pure causal conditions—characterized by being without fault, without entanglement, without obstruction, and having the mark of emptiness—and thus addresses him with such discourse.
If a bodhisattva, having heard this teaching, delights in dwelling in the world without weariness, until they achieve unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment.
At that time, the Venerable Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:

“The World-Honored One has spoken of three kinds of grave offenses of the three poisons—those associated with the condition of greed, those entangled by the condition of hatred, and those of delusion.”
"What is most grave? What is most light?
We pray that you will explain for the sake of bodhisattvas newly practicing the Mahāyāna the skillful means regarding their grave and light precepts."
At that time, the Buddha addressed the venerable Upāli, saying:

"If a bodhisattva who has first begun practicing the Mahāyāna were to constantly commit offenses of the nature of greed for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, yet another person, having faith in and accepting the Mahāyāna, were to give rise to a single thought of anger, the gravity of the offense resulting from that anger would outweigh that of greed."
Why is this? Upāli!
If a mind of anger is aroused, one is then able to abandon sentient beings.
If one abandons anger and greed, and when the mind of desire arises, one gathers in sentient beings, then the bodhisattva will encounter no calamities or difficulties.
Why is this? Upāli!
The Buddha taught that if one commits an offense of greed, the transgression is somewhat light if one abandons it and distances oneself from it somewhat slowly;
if one commits an offense of anger, the transgression is very heavy even if one resolves and detaches from it somewhat quickly;
and if one commits an offense of delusion, although one may resolve and detach from it quickly, the offense incurred is somewhat deep.
Upāli, you should know that the gravity of the three poisons is thus; a practicing bodhisattva should guard the mind of skillful means and wisdom so as not to commit any transgression.

Eleventh, the eleventh chapter from the *Sarvavastu-viśuddha-vinaya-sūtra*, which clearly explains the practice of two rules: it interprets how the practices of Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas each discipline their minds, categorized according to the relative gravity of the two vehicles.
At that time, the Devaputra Śāntaviśuddhi addressed the youth Mañjuśrī, saying:
"How does a bodhisattva who has first begun their practice discipline their mind?
And how does a śrāvaka bhikṣu discipline his mind?"
Mañjuśrī replied: "To feel weary of and detached from the triple world because the mind is agitated by it constitutes the taming of the mind of a śrāvaka.

However, to embrace the immeasurable dharmas of the world, not severing the cycle of birth and death, bestowing fearlessness upon all sentient beings, and joyfully dwelling in the world for the sake of benefiting them—this is the taming of the mind of a practicing bodhisattva."
"If one becomes weary of the accumulation of the provisions for merit, that is the disciplining of the mind of a śrāvaka;
if one never tires of accumulating the provisions for wisdom and merit, that is the disciplining of the mind of a practicing bodhisattva."
"If one feels weary of seeing all afflictions, that is the śrāvaka taming his mind;
if one gathers in the afflictions of all sentient beings, that is the bodhisattva practicing the taming of his mind."
"If one does not contemplate the noble virtues of the Buddhas for the sake of sentient beings, then that is the mental discipline of a śrāvaka;
if one manifests the noble virtues of the Buddhas for the sake of all sentient beings, then that is the mental discipline of a practicing bodhisattva."
"If the various devas do not witness the deeds one practices, then it is a śrāvaka taming his mind;
if, moreover, the deeds one practices are universally witnessed, known, and heard by the devas of the trichiliocosm, then it is a practicing bodhisattva taming his mind."
"If one abandons all the armies of Māra, that is the śrāvaka taming his mind;
if one is able to subdue all the armies of Māra throughout the trichiliocosm when they are mobilized, that is the bodhisattva practicing the taming of his mind."
"If one does not understand the measure of one's own mind, that is the Śrāvaka taming his mind;
if one understands all Buddha-lands and the noble virtues of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas, that is the Bodhisattva practicing to tame his mind."
"If it is solely for one's own sake, then it is the Śrāvaka’s cultivation of mind-discipline;
if, for the sake of sentient beings, one practices the cultivation of mindfulness of all the noble virtues of the Buddhas, then it is the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of mind-discipline."
"If one is attached to the swift liberation of the Hīnayāna, then that is the Śrāvaka taming his mind;
if one brings bodhi to maturity through momentary wisdom, then that is the Bodhisattva practicing to tame his mind."
"If one cuts off the lineage of the Three Jewels, that is the śrāvaka’s disciplining of the mind;
if one cultivates and studies the lineage of the Three Jewels, that is the bodhisattva’s practice of disciplining the mind."
"If it is likened to a clay jar that has been broken and can never be restored to its original state, this represents the Śrāvaka’s disciplining of the mind;
if it is likened to a golden vessel that, though broken, is repaired and restored to its former condition, this represents the Bodhisattva practitioner’s disciplining of the mind."
"If one lacks skillful means, then it is the discipline of the mind of a śrāvaka;
if one is endowed with skillful means, then it is the discipline of the mind of a practicing bodhisattva."
"If one does not possess the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses, then it is a śrāvaka taming their mind;
if one's mind is conjoined with the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses, then it is a practicing bodhisattva taming their mind."
"If one avoids the world as one would avoid a pit of fire, that is the śrāvaka taming his mind;
if one delights in dwelling in the world as if wandering through a garden or residing in a palace, that is the practicing bodhisattva taming his mind."
"If one does not possess the six pāramitās along with the four means of attraction (saṃgrahavastu), then one is a śrāvaka taming the mind;
if one cultivates the six pāramitās along with the four means of attraction, firmly maintaining and gathering mindfulness, then one is a bodhisattva practicing the taming of the mind."
"If one does not sever all habitual tendencies from past conditions, that is the Śrāvaka’s disciplining of the mind;
if one eliminates all habitual tendencies within the continuum, that is the Bodhisattva practitioner’s disciplining of the mind."
"To state it briefly:

if the mind clings to finite numbers and associates with finite dharmas—practicing finite precepts, samādhi, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation—then this is a śrāvaka taming the mind.

If, however, one does not rely on finite numbers but is bound by the infinite, associating with infinite skillful means, and if the precepts, samādhi, wisdom, and liberation that are practiced further take as their object the vision of liberation, then this is a bodhisattva practicing to tame the mind."
At that time, the Tathāgata addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
“Excellent, excellent! It is as you have said;
this is the practice for a bodhisattva’s initial entry into the dharma-practice of disciplining the mind.”
For what reason? Mañjuśrī!
Listen to my explanation, even unto liberation; for this meaning of discipline should be largely accomplished and perfected.
Mañjuśrī! It is as if two people were dwelling in the same place; one person praises the waters of the four great oceans, while the other praises the water in a cow’s footprint.
Mañjuśrī! What do you think? Is the water in a cow’s footprint worthy of much praise?
Mañjuśrī said, "This pit is shallow and slight; how could it possibly be comparable to the four great oceans in terms of the weight of its praise?
The Buddha said:

"If the manifestations of the Śrāvakas' discipline are likewise like this—just as the swirling water in a cow's footprint is meager by nature and provides no benefit or praise—one should know that the gravity of the Lesser Vehicle is just like this."
"Mañjuśrī, suppose there were a person who praised the great ocean;
what do you think—
would that person be capable of praising the great ocean?"
Mañjuśrī said, “The virtues of the great ocean are immeasurable; its praises are immeasurable.
The Buddha said:

“The cultivation of a bodhisattva is also like this: one should manifest immeasurable cultivation, just as the great ocean cannot be measured by the number of drops; the merits of the Mahāyāna are likewise so.”
At that time, when this Dharma had been taught, twelve thousand devaputras all resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and each spoke these words:
“World-Honored One!
"From this day forth, we shall practice and train in the sphere of the bodhisattva’s conduct; may we lead all sentient beings to enter this path.

Translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Zhiyan of Zhixiang Monastery during the Great Tang Dynasty. Part Twelve:
From the *Sūtra Spoken by Bodhisattva Sāgaramati*, Revealing the Eightfold Practice; Explaining how a bodhisattva who has transgressed the precepts can still accomplish the six pāramitās.
To understand the profound meaning of the *prajñāpāramitā* and to weigh the relative gravity of the śrāvaka path;
to understand the jewel-like patience of one who has first resolved upon bodhicitta, whereby even māras cannot cause them to retreat from awakening.
He understands how the three karmas of body, speech, and mind accomplish the six *pāramitās*.
He understands the gateway of mindfulness for accomplishing the six *pāramitās* through contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*).
He understands the analogy of the eight kinds of merit being intermingled with afflictions (*kleśa*).
He explained the gateway of the four kinds of wholesome conduct.
He explained that the gateway of the bodhisattva’s practice contains twelve hooks of demonic obstacles.
At that time, a certain devaputra addressed the youth Mañjuśrī, saying:
“Mañjuśrī! Is it possible for a bodhisattva who has newly begun their practice and harbors a mind of stinginess to accomplish the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā)? Mañjuśrī replied:
“There is such a practitioner.
The Son of Heaven asked,
“By what principle does such a person exist?”
Mañjuśrī said: "If a practicing bodhisattva brings sentient beings to maturity, they do not abandon bodhi;
because they do not abandon it, this is stinginess."
"Because one matures sentient beings through the mind of giving, one is then able to accomplish the dāna-pāramitā.
Furthermore, the devaputra addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Is it possible for a bodhisattva who practices to accomplish the śīla-pāramitā even while violating the precepts?"
Mañjuśrī said, “There is such a practitioner.
The devaputra addressed him, saying:
"For what reason does such a person exist?

Mañjuśrī replied, "Because they practice the bodhisattva path to gather, protect, and bring sentient beings to maturity; thus, even if they do not possess [ordinary] precepts, they achieve the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā)."
Furthermore, the devaputra addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Is it possible for a bodhisattva practicing the path to abandon patience and yet still achieve the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā)?"
Mañjuśrī replied, “There is such a practitioner. The devaputra said:
"For what reason does such a person exist? Mañjuśrī replied,

"If a practicing bodhisattva abandons the practices of non-Buddhists and exclusively cultivates the patience regarding the Dharma of unsurpassed enlightenment, they thereby achieve the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā)."
Furthermore, the devaputra addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Is it possible for a bodhisattva who practices with arrogance and conceit to achieve perfection in the pāramitā of diligence?"
Mañjuśrī said, "There is such a practitioner.
The devaputra addressed him, saying:
"For what reason does such a person exist? Mañjuśrī replied:

"If a practicing bodhisattva does not delight in the fruits of a pratyekabuddha or an arhat, but rather, for the sake of manifesting the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñā-jñāna*), delights in the Mahāyāna with an untiring mind, and accumulates virtuous thoughts toward unsurpassed bodhi, they thereby achieve the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*)."
Furthermore, the devaputra addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Is it possible for a bodhisattva who practices with a distracted mind to achieve accomplishment in the dhyāna-pāramitā?"
Mañjuśrī said, "There is such a practitioner.
The devaputra addressed him, saying:
"For what reason does such a person exist? Mañjuśrī replied,

"If a bodhisattva practices until even in sleep they take no pleasure in the fruits of pratyekabuddhahood or arhatship, but instead single-mindedly seeks unsurpassed bodhi and thereby achieves the perfection of dhyāna."
Furthermore, the devaputra addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Is it possible for a bodhisattva who practices with folly and lacks wisdom to achieve the perfection of prajñā?"
Mañjuśrī said: "There is such a practitioner.
The devaputra addressed him, saying:
"For what reason does such a person exist? Mañjuśrī replied:

"If a bodhisattva’s cultivation of wisdom is narrow and inferior, and they encounter worldly sorcery, incantations, the stirring of *vetāla* spirits, or the unsettling of others' minds, yet the bodhisattva lacks the skillful means and wisdom to rescue and protect them—nevertheless, for the sake of the bodhicitta, they embrace mindfulness of the Buddha-lands and thereby achieve the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*)."
At that time, the Tathāgata praised Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, saying: “Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī!”

It is exactly as you have said; that you are able to distinguish between what should and should not be practiced by a bodhisattva in the initial stage of cultivation is truly and not falsely so. Why is this?
Listen now as I briefly explain the perfection of the *prajñāpāramitā* and complete liberation.
Mañjuśrī, it is like a person who, for the space of a single day, endures hunger but does not taste poisoned food.

The practice of a bodhisattva is likewise: it is better to maintain stinginess, lack of precept-keeping, anger, indolence, and a lack of mental composure, than to delight in the practices of the paths of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
If the mind delights in practicing the six pāramitās, it should not be so.
Why is this? Because within these [practices], the bodhisattva ought to encounter obstacles.
The devaputra said:
“World-Honored One!
A bodhisattva who practices should not fear the afflictions.”
The Buddha said, “A practicing bodhisattva truly fears afflictions, for they dread falling into the stage of a śrāvaka.
O Son of Heaven! ”
"What do you think?

Suppose there were a person whose primary concern was their own life, and they were suddenly subjected to violence; would they rather have their head cut off, or would they rather have their body cut?"
The devaputra said:
“World-Honored One!
If one wishes to preserve one’s life, one would rather cut the flesh from one’s body than sever one’s head.”
Why is this? If its head is preserved, it can still cultivate and accumulate the traces of merit and virtue; because of these virtuous traces, it will be reborn in the heavens.
If its head is severed, those virtuous traces are extinguished along with it.
The Buddha told the devaputra:
"The practice of a bodhisattva is likewise: it is better to abandon dignified deportment and preceptual conduct than to retreat from bodhi;
it is better to remain associated with afflictions than to enter the gate of severing afflictions followed by the śrāvakas."
The devaputra said:
“World-Honored One!
That a bodhisattva practices such deeds and conducts is rare in the world and extremely difficult to believe.”
“The diligent practice of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is like a bodhisattva practicing while violating the precepts.
The Buddha said,
“It is exactly as you have said.”
For example, if the ordinary food of a poor household were tasted even briefly by a Wheel-Turning King, it would be like ingesting poison.
Likewise, when a śrāvaka eliminates afflictions with firm diligence, it is similar to the practice of a bodhisattva’s ethical discipline.
"Furthermore, it is like a person who diligently seeks a livelihood and adorns their body; such a person cannot even sustain the wealth of an entire kingdom, let alone that of the rest of the world."

The śrāvakas are likewise; because they have eliminated only their own afflictions, although they practice with diligence, they are incapable of benefiting the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa, let alone those of other worlds.

"Furthermore, it is like a great and wealthy merchant leader who has many kinsmen, attendants, and followers; with a diligent mind and a love for giving, he is able to benefit immeasurable sentient beings."
"Son of Heaven, you should know:

the practice of a bodhisattva is likewise thus. Cultivating loving-kindness and compassion, and exerting himself with a compassionate mind, he thereby benefits all sentient beings, extensively bestowing happiness upon them through both the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) and the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya)."
At that time, the Elder Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If a śrāvaka cultivates the path to realize the fruit of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), whereas a bodhisattva practices within the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), by what principle is it that the practicing bodhisattva is able to surpass those who have realized the fruit of the unconditioned?”
The Buddha said, “Kāśyapa,
you should know that I shall provide a simile for you, for the wise understand quickly through similes.
Suppose there were four great oceans filled with ghee, and a person took a single cow’s hair, divided it into one hundred parts, and used the tip of one such part to take a single drop of that ghee.”
Kāśyapa, what do you think?
Is the amount of ghee contained in that single drop on the tip of a hair more than the ghee in those four great oceans?
Kāśyapa replied, “No, World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said: "Kāśyapa, what do you think?"
"Between these two portions of ghee, which is the most superior, the most venerable, the most abundant, and the most precious?

Kāśyapa replied, "If one were to compare a portion of ghee on the tip of a single hair to the ghee of the great ocean, exceeding hundreds of thousands of millions, that ghee would indeed be the most superior, the most venerable, the most abundant, and the most precious; a single drop of that [oceanic] ghee cannot be compared to it."
The Buddha said: “Kāśyapa!

It is like the amount of ghee that could be obtained from the tip of a hair divided into a hundred parts; if a śrāvaka’s unconditioned wisdom were compared to the wisdom of a buddha, it would be just like that.”
The practicing bodhisattva cultivates conditioned merits and unconditioned vows, universally entering the wisdom of the Buddha.
Kāśyapa, you should know:
it is like the species of mosquitoes and ants, which can obtain only a single grain of food for their sustenance.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, suppose there were a person who extensively planted field crops for three months.
What do you think? Which of these two would be more numerous?
Kāśyapa said: "If what is sown for three months reaches harvest in the autumn, its quantity will be immeasurable, bringing great benefit to sentient beings.
Yet even a single grain of food cannot yet benefit oneself, let alone benefit sentient beings."
The Buddha said:
"Kāśyapa, you should know:
for example, it is like a mosquito or an ant holding a single grain of food; the śrāvaka is just like that."
If one sows extensively for three months, the harvest will be very abundant.

It is the same with the merit of a practicing bodhisattva regarding the six pāramitās and the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*): once it has matured, they establish the benefit of immeasurable sentient beings, universally bestowing happiness through both the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) and conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*), and thereby achieve unsurpassed nirvāṇa.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

"Suppose there were a lapis lazuli gem worth hundreds of thousands of loads that entered a city; yet, suppose there were another priceless jewel placed within a ship upon the great ocean, which, if unimpeded, reaches Jambudvīpa. This jewel would universally enrich the beings of Jambudvīpa and benefit those who are poor and suffering."
Kāśyapa, what do you think?
Could the total value of those hundreds of thousands of vaiḍūrya beads possibly exceed that of this single precious gem?
Kāśyapa replied, “No, World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said:
"Because those lapis lazuli beads have no value, the śrāvakas' cultivation of entry into unconditioned liberation is likewise so.
Kāśyapa, you should know this:"
For example, it is like a priceless jewel still upon a ship at sea; if there are no obstacles and it reaches Jambudvīpa, it can universally enrich all sentient beings.

If a practicing bodhisattva ensures that the lineage of the Three Jewels continues without interruption and is able to give rise to unsurpassed bodhi, this is analogous to obtaining a precious jewel that brings benefit to immeasurable beings.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Sāgaramati Bodhisattva, saying:
"How is it that one who has first produced the jewel of the bodhicitta is able to practice patience and not regress from bodhi?"
How can there be obstacles to the jewel of the bodhicitta?
Sāgaramati, you should know this:

if a practicing bodhisattva, having already generated the bodhicitta, encounters an evil friend—whether it be Māra Pāpīyān, or a member of Māra’s retinue, or one who serves false deities, or one who dwells in demonic conduct—and is thereby harassed and robbed of their wholesome mind, the mind of that practicing bodhisattva will become doubtful.

When such demonic adversaries come to harass the Bodhisattva, at that time the Bodhisattva’s mind does not waver or retreat; he neither distances himself from unexcelled bodhi nor severs the liberation of sentient beings. Out of great compassion, he diligently cultivates and accumulates [merit], never severing the lineage of the Triple Gem, never severing all Buddha-activities, and never severing the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics. He practices in successive stages, manifesting and accumulating the provisions of merit, and manifesting pure Buddha-fields. Because he protects and upholds the wholesome Dharma through cultivation and study, he sacrifices his own body and life to bring sentient beings to maturity, taking no pleasure in the defiled attachments of worldly happiness.

If a practicing bodhisattva, for the sake of sentient beings, maintains firm resolve through great compassion and patience, being able to endure unspeakable insults and contempt from others, as well as all forms of suffering such as beatings and blows; if they can shoulder the heavy burden of sentient beings without hiding or shrinking back, persevering without retreat, their mind courageous and reaching the other shore without weariness; and if they cultivate diligence, give rise to skillful means, and remain steadfast in single-minded devotion—[this is the perfection of patience].
If others cause him distress, he does not distress them in return;
if someone strikes or reviles him, he does not harbor anger toward them.
For the sake of the Mahāyāna meaning, he distinguishes himself from the world, and with right mindfulness, this mind deliberates upon the path of goodness:
"For the sake of sentient beings, I have followed the ways of the three realms; now I diligently seek to practice the contrary way.
Since the sentient beings of the three realms oppose or comply with me, I should accord with them and harmonize with them.
While these beings possess fierce and violent anger, I seek patience and maintain a mind of compliance."
"The sentient beings of the world deceive and delude one another; I now contemplate only the perfection of wisdom.
If sentient beings from the ten directions were to assemble and each carry weapons—swords, blades, spears, and lances—and follow me, each harboring this thought:

"Whether this practicing bodhisattva is walking, standing, sitting, or lying down; whether he has generated the mind of awakening, or the mind of giving, or the mind of ethical discipline, or the mind of patience, or the mind of diligence, or the mind of meditative concentration, or the mind of wisdom, or the mind of studying the sūtras, or the mind of cultivating and maintaining merit—when this practicing bodhisattva is mindful of such a mind, we shall then sever his head and cut his body into pieces as small as jujube leaves."
"These sentient beings harbor nothing but anger and are intent on killing.
At that time, the practicing Bodhisattva focuses his mind and reflects:
'I now have no heart of resentment toward others; through patience, I am free from enmity and malice.'"
For what reason?

This body of mine has, since beginningless time within the three realms, undergone an infinite number of births and deaths through successive transformations; there is no place it has not experienced, passing through the hells, the realm of hungry ghosts, and the animal realm, where it has endured immeasurable suffering.
At times born among humans, it has never for a moment relinquished its craving for the five desires, or has followed the hearts of others by listening to what is not the Dharma.

For this reason, though I may unjustly lose my life and have my limbs severed and my body divided into a hundred pieces, even during such times of suffering, neither you nor I shall derive any mutual benefit.
Now that you have cut my limbs and severed my life-force, if you can continue this without ceasing for as long as the kalpas of the future endure, I shall never abandon unsurpassed bodhi.
For what reason?

The agony of having my limbs severed and mutilated that I now endure is more than a hundred times greater than the sufferings of hell; yet I vow to enter hell rather than abandon bodhicitta, so that through great compassion I may deliver all sentient beings.
Why is this? As the Tathāgata has taught:
even a small measure of mental capacity can accomplish great deeds.
In this world, sentient beings have many evil friends and very few virtuous friends; you should know that one ought not to take an evil friend as a companion.
Why is this? Because I harbor no enmity or malice toward sentient beings, nor do I give rise to a heart of resentment.
"He gives to others, while I give to him;
he alone harbors anger and jealousy toward others, while I alone offer them loving-kindness and patience.
I should now manifest the power of non-killing and patience, and the power of not giving rise to anger; if I can sacrifice my body and life, I shall swiftly attain unimpeded Bodhi."
"Regarding the body, one is defiled by craving for the five desires; once life has ended, one must eliminate all anger within oneself.
If it should arise, one should abandon it through mindfulness and eliminate it.

"If one can enter this Dharma-gate, you should know that a Bodhisattva practicing in this way is able to endure the afflictions and disturbances caused by all sentient beings, does not sever ties with them, and is always able to practice patience toward the three kinds of suffering."
What are these three? They are:
first, patience regarding physical affliction; second, patience regarding verbal affliction; and third, patience regarding mental affliction.
"Furthermore, what is patience regarding bodily affliction?
It is when one is able to endure having one's body cut, contemplating sentient beings who have their bodies cut as merely the mental phenomena of the world."

If a practicing bodhisattva, while employing wisdom and skillful means, contemplates the six pāramitās at the very moment of cutting their own body, they thus contemplate the mind in relinquishing body, life, and wealth.
By giving up one’s body and life, and by not being stingy with one’s person, one can accomplish the practice of the *dānapāramitā*.

If one should be harmed, through the universality of a compassionate heart, even though there is physical pain, the mind remains undisturbed; thus, one can accomplish the practice of the *śīlapāramitā*.

If, when one's body is being dismembered, one vows to deliver this person by enduring it without seeking recompense, then one can accomplish the practice of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).

If, through firm diligence and by not abandoning the bodhicitta, one does not grow weary of the world and cultivates all manner of meritorious virtues, then one can accomplish the practice of the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
When the body is being dismembered, one should collect the mind and reflect:
"This body is like grass, wood, tiles, stones, shadows, or walls; it is illusory, impermanent, and without self, perishing in an instant."
Having observed in this way, one is able to accomplish the practice of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

Sāgaramati, you should know that if a practicing bodhisattva employs such skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), they will be able to fulfill the practices of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) without retreating from awakening; this is the bodhisattva’s accomplishment of the practice of patience regarding the body (*kāya-kṣānti*).
"Furthermore, what is the bodhisattva’s practice of patience regarding verbal affliction?

If a practicing bodhisattva is reviled with unspeakable words, or encounters all manner of strife, anger, resentment, contempt, beating, or improper speech—whether right or wrong—and upon hearing such harsh words from others, does not give rise to anger or enmity but is able to endure them all, this is the bodhisattva’s accomplishment of the practice of patience regarding speech."
"Furthermore, how does a practicing bodhisattva cultivate patience toward the intent to cause disturbance?
If a practicing bodhisattva, being endowed with skillful means and wisdom, is reviled, insulted, or subjected to unspeakable anger and reproach by others."
When a bodhisattva has heard this and is able to endure it in mind, they are practicing the bodhisattva’s accomplishment of the practice of mental patience.
"Furthermore, Sāgaramati!

How does a bodhisattva practice the gateway of mindfulness through the cultivation of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) and perfected wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*) so as to accomplish the contemplative practices (*vipaśyanā-bhāvanā*) of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*)?

If a practicing bodhisattva hears another revile him—with words that are difficult to hear, difficult to endure, and abusive or angry beyond description—the bodhisattva should contemplate that person in this way:

"This person who reviles me now must have been stingy, jealous, and deprived of favorable conditions in the past; they were not granted instruction nor did they ever make offerings to the Triple Gem. That they revile me now, I should now eliminate their afflictions (*kleśa*), anger, and resentment."

I shall now abandon resentment, malice, and envy; free from greed and attachment, I will seek out virtuous friends, cultivate the path of goodness, attend upon those who are good, and restrain the faults of speech.
"Then one can accomplish the dānapāramitā.
Furthermore, a practicing bodhisattva should form this thought:
'This person violates the precepts and does not recognize their transgression;'"
"I have already received the precepts; I should not give way to anger or agitation.
By single-mindedly recollecting the Buddha and contemplating the retribution for one's offenses, one can thus accomplish the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*).
"Furthermore, a practicing bodhisattva should think:
'This person reviles me because their habitual nature is full of anger and malice;
I, however, am now without resentment and direct toward them a heart of loving-kindness.'"
Thus, one is able to accomplish the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
Furthermore, a practicing bodhisattva should reflect:
"This person lacks virtuous conduct; that is why they revile me."
I shall now exert myself with body and mind, maintaining single-minded right mindfulness and never forgetting bodhi.

Because these evil people have benefited me, they have formed a great causal connection for me; those who are not yet tamed, I shall cause to be tamed; those who do not yet contemplate goodness, I shall cause to contemplate goodness; and those who do not yet cease from evil, I shall cause to cease from evil.
With such a mental attitude, one is able to accomplish the dhyāna-pāramitā.
Furthermore, a practicing bodhisattva should form this thought: "This person is autonomous yet lacks wisdom;
they cling to the perception of signs, the perception of a self, the perception of a sentient being, and the perception of greedily accepting wealth, and for this reason they revile me."
I now reflect upon this according to the Dharma: who is there within this?
Who is it that reviles?
Both the giver and the receiver are non-existent.

Since there is neither self nor other, one is able to eliminate all erroneous practices regarding the characteristics of phenomena; being without enmity and capable of patience, one then achieves the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
The Buddha told Sāgaramati Bodhisattva:

“If a practicing bodhisattva, by virtue of possessing wisdom, hears the harsh words, insults, and slanders of others—speech that is unbearable to hear—and is nevertheless able to endure them with composure, then their vows and practices will be fulfilled, they will achieve the concentration of the pāramitās, they will not depart from the Mahāyāna, and they will thus accomplish the patience of enduring verbal affliction.”
At that time, Sāgaramati Bodhisattva said:
"What is the bodhisattva’s practice of patience toward the intention to cause affliction?
It is when all demonic obstacles cause that bodhisattva to distance themselves from bodhi and urge them to give rise to a mind of regression."
All non-Buddhists, out of greed for gain and offerings, practice erroneous conduct, causing Bodhisattvas to distance themselves from Bodhi.

However, a Bodhisattva who has already realized correct practice possesses a mind free from distraction and does not depart from Bodhi; even when manifesting the body of a Buddha, their mind remains without retreat or fluctuation.
Furthermore, there are powerful malevolent spirits who rebuke the Bodhisattva to give rise to false thoughts, saying to him:

"You do not possess the power to gather the Mahāyāna; you shall never become a Buddha. Quickly cast off this heavy burden and abandon this diligence! Enlightenment is difficult to attain, and the holy virtue of a Tathāgata is likewise hard to seek."

"In this world there are immeasurable sufferings and afflictions difficult to endure; those who have already entered nirvana now experience happiness. You, O Great Being, should likewise enter nirvana swiftly."
“Sāgaramati, you should know this:
when a bodhisattva practicing the path is being urged to retreat from enlightenment, the bodhisattva does not follow the wishes of others and does not abandon right mindfulness.”
The Bodhisattva forms this thought:

"I shall certainly sit beneath the Bodhi tree; I shall certainly crush and subdue the hosts of demonic armies; I shall certainly attain equal and perfect enlightenment and turn the Great Wheel of Dharma, expounding the Buddha-dharma throughout the trichiliocosm."
I have already exhorted all sentient beings to attain perfect enlightenment, universally wishing that they may receive from me the gift of pure Dharma.

If all Buddhas and the noble sages with knowledge of others' minds perceive my sincere resolve for bodhi and my vows, then by virtue of this bodhicitta, I shall practice patience regarding my own body; I dare not deceive or delude the Buddhas, the noble sages, all sentient beings, or even myself.
"Practicing in this way, the bodhisattva gathers the mind and endures, neither regressing from the Mahāyāna nor severing the jewel of the bodhicitta.

Saṃudgata, you should know that by thus giving rise to the jewel of bodhicitta, one is able to give rise to the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) and further avoid retreating from the perfection of diligence (vīrya-pāramitā). To fulfill these two practices is the bodhisattva’s mental endurance toward affliction."
At that time, Sāgaramati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is it that constitutes the continuity of worldly merit which, though mixed with afflictions, is able to bring beings to maturity?”
"For what reason, World-Honored One, are we sentient beings called the 'continuum of the world' wherein merit and afflictions are intermingled?
The Buddha said,
"There are eight kinds of worldly continuums wherein merit and afflictions are intermingled."
What are the eight? They are:
first, never being weary of cultivating the bodhisattva’s provisions of merit;
Second, delighting in the cycle of birth and death within the world;
third, aspiring to encounter all Buddhas and Tathāgatas;
fourth, aspiring to bring sentient beings to maturity without weariness.
Fifth, to protect the Buddha-dharma by practicing and studying it;
sixth, to diligently gather and guide sentient beings toward wholesome conduct;
seventh, to take profound delight in the Buddha-dharma and never abandon bodhicitta.
Eighth, they practice the perfections with attachment yet possess no mind of renunciation.
Sāgaramati, you should know that while such worldly continuity involves a mixture of merit and afflictions in practice, this practice of the bodhisattva is untainted by evil views or afflictions.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How can these various merits be mixed with afflictions?
The Buddha said:

"You should know that the three realms established herein are all brought into existence by afflictions (*kleśa*). Yet, bodhisattvas who practice with skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) and the power of merit vow to dwell in the world to rescue and deliver sentient beings; they thus constantly remain within the three realms, embracing afflictions."
“Because the bodhisattva does not act for his own sake, as his agitation is profound, for this reason, his merit is intermingled with afflictions.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
Such immeasurable bodhisattva practices and vows, relying upon the inconceivable wisdom and skillful means of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas, are most rare and difficult to encounter.
World-Honored One!

Furthermore, one sees bodhisattvas who have first begun their practice—acting for the sake of the Tathāgata’s wisdom—engaging in immeasurable and diverse types of karmic activities according to the needs of sentient beings; these are exceedingly difficult, most difficult, and cannot even be heard or described.
“If a practicing bodhisattva performs such difficult practices and endures such hardships without being startled or afraid, that matter is even more difficult.
When Śāriputra had finished speaking these words, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying: “Śāriputra!...”
"What do you think?
Would a lion cub feel fear or alarm upon hearing its father’s roar?
Śāriputra replied:
"No, World-Honored One. The Buddha said:
“Śāriputra, you should know:

if a practicing bodhisattva hears the lion’s roar of awakening and is neither startled nor afraid, and if they hear of the various and diverse, immeasurable karmic actions of sentient beings and remain neither startled nor shaken;”
Śāriputra! Just as a tiny spark does not fear any grasses, trees, or thickets, nor does it think:
"I lack the power to burn the grasses and trees of the world."
The practicing bodhisattva is also like this: using the small fire of wisdom to rescue all sentient beings, they do not fear any afflictions, nor do they think:
"I am incapable of eliminating the afflictions of the world of sentient beings."
"Why is this? If one clearly recognizes the afflictions of all sentient beings, these very afflictions assist the torch of wisdom.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"It is like this: suppose all the grasses, trees, branches, leaves, roots, and stalks in the world were to say to one another, 'Seven days from now, let all the grasses and trees engage in a battle with fire; each shall strive for victory.'"
At that time, these various grasses and trees were piled up as a heap of firewood as high as Mount Sumeru. Someone addressed the fire, saying:
"This accumulation of firewood is as high as Mount Sumeru; why do you, O Fire, not gather your strength?"
"It will surely be overcome by the brushwood.
The Fire said,
"I do not gather a multitude."
Why is this? Grasses and trees are my friends;
if grasses and trees are abundant, I shall possess strength.
"If the grass and trees are few, I shall then be extinguished.

Śāriputra, it is the same for a bodhisattva who practices the path: because sentient beings possess immeasurable afflictions, they are able to cause the torch of wisdom to blaze brightly, and the power of the practicing bodhisattva gradually increases.
If one has clearly understood the meaning of afflictions and yet takes those afflictions as the torch of wisdom;
whereas if a practicing bodhisattva does not delight in afflictions but abandons them, they will fall to the level of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Śāriputra, you should know this:
if a practicing bodhisattva observes all afflictions with right mindfulness, the power of that practicing bodhisattva will gradually become strong.
If, upon hearing these words, one is neither startled nor shaken, you should know that this bodhisattva has achieved skillful means and wisdom.
"Furthermore, there are four types of corresponding wholesome practices for a practicing bodhisattva.
What are the four? They are as follows: "
First, to diligently cultivate the six pāramitās;
second, to bring sentient beings to maturity with a mind of great compassion;
third, to firmly maintain meritorious virtues until they are fully perfected.
Fourth, for immeasurable eons, one protects the three realms without weariness and accumulates all the provisions of merit.
If a practicing bodhisattva can accomplish these four kinds of merit, they constitute the definitive conduct of a bodhisattva.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati, saying: "Good son,
do you recognize the māra Pāpīyān, Aṅkuśa?"
The Bodhisattva Sāgaramati said:
“World-Honored One!
I recognize this as the hook of demonic obstacles.”
The Buddha said,
“Do you now wish to hear the meaning of liberation from the hook of demonic obstacles?
Sāgaramati Bodhisattva replied:
"I wish to hear it with joy.
The Buddha said,

"If there are bodhisattvas who, having heard this meaning, attain liberation from the hooks of the obstacles of malevolent spirits and demons, they will be able to crush and subdue all demonic armies and swiftly achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We now wish, through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, to speak concerning the twelve kinds of māra-ākṣepa-hooks for the sake of those who first practice the path of the bodhisattvas."
What are the twelve? They are as follows:

First, when a practicing bodhisattva cultivates the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā), they feel stinginess toward things they love and are only able to relinquish and give away things they do not love.
"If there are those who are relatives or acquaintances, one intends to give;
if they are not relatives or acquaintances, the mind has no inclination to relinquish.
Both giver and recipient give rise to discrimination, World-Honored One!"
This is the first obstacle for a practicing bodhisattva—the demon’s hook of stinginess.

Furthermore, World-Honored One, if a practicing bodhisattva practices wholesome diligence, firmly maintains the precepts, and is fully endowed with dignified deportment, then even for minor transgressions, they perceive and acknowledge their faults; thus, body and mind are pure, and they practice the precepts with equanimity.
If one sees a bhikṣu or a brāhmaṇa who is diligent and gives rise to the thought of making offerings to them, one associates with and trains alongside them;
yet, if one sees someone who violates the precepts, one gives rise to anger, harbors resentment, and treats them with contempt.
"To praise one's own practice and disparage others, World-Honored One!
This is the second obstacle for a practicing bodhisattva—the demon’s hook of maintaining precepts.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!"
If a practicing bodhisattva possesses patience of body and patience of speech, yet lacks patience of mind, they instead give rise to anger.
If they see those who rely on powerful clans, they will proclaim their virtues and exercise patience toward them;
however, if they see those of lowly or common status, they give rise to resentment and lack a patient heart.
"Although they may temporarily endure with composure, their minds harbor arrogance and they do not relinquish anger.
World-Honored One!
This is the third obstacle for a practicing bodhisattva—the demon’s hook of patience."
"Furthermore, World-Honored One,
if a practicing bodhisattva diligently studies and trains to transform sentient beings, leading them into the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas rather than teaching them the Mahāyāna;
and if they praise the stages of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha;"
They devote themselves exclusively to conventional truth while abandoning the gateway of the ultimate truth;
they conceal the Mahāyāna and focus solely on worldly fame and profit;
they seek renown by offering banners, streamers, music, flowers, and incense to the sacred image, yet they do not peruse the Mahāyāna nor seek the Buddha-dharma.
“World-Honored One!
This is the fourth obstacle for a practicing bodhisattva—the demon’s hook of diligence.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!”

If a practicing bodhisattva gives rise to the four dhyānas and samāpattis, remaining in silent meditative seclusion and achieving concentration, yet disparages the places where sentient beings are brought to maturity, disparages the teaching of the Buddha-dharma, disparages dwelling together with sentient beings, and disparages the performance of wholesome conditioned merits—remaining unmoved by unconditioned dharmas and practicing them only slightly, while not seeking such meditative concentration.
Looking back, they see the desire realm and the formless realm; delighting in the formless heavens, because their faculties are dull, they aspire for a long life.

If they are born in the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*), even though hundreds of thousands of Buddhas attain equal and perfect enlightenment, such persons have no way to encounter these Buddhas, hear the Buddha-dharma, or meet the Saṅgha. They cannot bring sentient beings to maturity, nor do they encounter or receive the Tathāgata’s sublime Dharma, nor do they encounter the accumulation of the provisions of merit; thus they lack wisdom and are characterized by folly and indolence.
"World-Honored One, if one’s lifespan in the Heaven of No-Thought comes to an end and one is reborn in a lower realm, one will possess little wisdom and be weak.
World-Honored One,
this is the fifth obstacle for a practicing bodhisattva— the demon’s hook of meditative concentration."

"Furthermore, World-Honored One, if a practicing bodhisattva’s wisdom becomes increasingly expansive, yet distinguishes the nature of habitual tendencies and understands dependent origination, such that they do not establish, practice, or abide in anything, and consequently disparage conditioned merits, they will thereby lose their skillful means and wisdom."
If one does not practice generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, or meditative concentration, but praises only the Prajñāpāramitā, saying of oneself:
"Prajñā is supreme."

If one gives rise to conceptual discrimination regarding the five pāramitās, fails to gather sentient beings through the four means of attraction (saṃgrahavastu), and constantly regards the signless and the unconditioned as supreme, such a person—because their wisdom is not yet mature—will instead fall into a wrong path.
“World-Honored One!
This is the sixth obstacle for a practicing bodhisattva—the demon’s hook of prajñā.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!”
If a practicing bodhisattva cultivates the conduct of an araṇya-dweller, delighting in dwelling in tranquility, living alone in mountain forests without any attachment or craving;

being utterly without stores of provisions, neither residing among the laity nor the monastics; employing little effort or wisdom, remaining unmoving and at ease; neither studying profound meanings, nor maturing sentient beings, nor hearing the Buddha-dharma, nor investigating the path to be traversed; and if there is a place where profound meanings are being expounded, neither going there to listen, nor seeking to inquire about the profound teachings, nor searching for virtuous friends—[this is called the practice of an araṇya-dweller].
Because he delights in dwelling in an araṇya, his resolve remains unshaken by afflictions; yet, unless he excises the seeds of affliction, he will not reach even the Eightfold Noble Path.
"World-Honored One, although this practicing bodhisattva dwells in solitude, they do not benefit others nor themselves.
This, World-Honored One,
is the seventh obstacle for a practicing bodhisattva— the hook of the *āraṇya*-māra."

"Furthermore, World-Honored One, if a practicing bodhisattva preaches the Dharma with profound depth, pleasing and delightful speech, and gathers the assembly through majestic virtue, yet there are sentient beings capable of receiving the teaching whom they do not instruct, or if they see those of dull faculties and ignorance who are incapable of being taught and nevertheless manifest the Buddha-dharma to them— [this is a transgression]."
“World-Honored One!
This is the eighth hindrance for a practicing bodhisattva—the demonic hook of taking refuge in the ocean of the Dharma.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!”
If a practicing bodhisattva studies the secular treatises of non-Buddhist outsiders and abandons the profound meaning of the Mahāyāna, praising what the outsiders have said;
or if, seeing someone who is well-versed in non-Buddhist doctrines, they delight in speaking of them or listening to them, and extol this as a virtue.

At that time, there were among the assembly various hosts of devas who had come to the site of enlightenment because they delighted in hearing the Mahāyāna Dharma. Having heard the heterodox treatises being expounded, their hearts were filled with distress, and they returned to their own palaces, uttering these words:
"This son of good family has now extinguished the Dharma."
The Tathāgata has given excellent instruction; why then do Bodhisattvas who practice in this way as pillars of the Dharma instead teach worldly external treatises?
It is because they delight in frivolous discourse that they abandon the Mahāyāna.

Why is this? The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have attained perfect enlightenment for the sake of the profound Dharma; they do not achieve bodhi through the worldly conceptual proliferations of non-Buddhists.
"World-Honored One!

These practitioners of the Bodhisattva path study and expound the various doctrines of external paths, while concealing the Buddha-dharma of the Tathāgata. Such persons, within the Buddha-dharma, bring about the transformation into perfect enlightenment that exclusively practices annihilationism."
“World-Honored One!
This is the ninth obstacle for a practicing bodhisattva—the hook of Māra that covers the profound Buddha-dharma and extols the frivolous disputations of external paths.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!”

If a practicing bodhisattva follows an evil companion as a spiritual friend and forms a friendship with them, that evil friend will specifically cause the bodhisattva to abandon sentient beings and not bring them to maturity, nor will they cause him to support and protect the Buddha-dharma. They will instruct him to abide in a state of empty stillness requiring little effort, frequently teaching him the practices of the śrāvaka-dharma, and failing to proclaim any profound meanings corresponding to the Mahāyāna.

If a practicing bodhisattva, for the sake of training in the Mahāyāna, dwells in a place of tranquility desiring to advance toward enlightenment, an evil friend creates an obstacle, causing that bodhisattva to fixate upon worldly things and saying to him:
"A practicing bodhisattva ought to fixate upon worldly, mundane dharmas."

If they should be instructed in worldly dharmas, others cause them to abide in tranquility; for the purpose of manifesting and causing them to enter another stage, they do not reveal the gateways to the definitive, unsurpassed conduct of a bodhisattva.
“World-Honored One!
What is the bodhisattva’s gateway of the supreme practice of certainty?
It consists of ten kinds.”
What are the ten? They are as follows:
first, abiding in reliance upon the faculty of faith, because of receiving the instructions of spiritual friends;
Second, to seek the sublime Dharma with diligence as if one’s head were on fire;
third, to dwell joyfully in right mindfulness regarding the teachings of the wholesome Dharma and to constantly and diligently practice and study them;
fourth, to apply oneself with correct diligence and not abandon the mind once the task has been undertaken.
Fifth, they do not delight in their own happiness, but only aspire to bring sentient beings to maturity;
sixth, for the sake of seeking the Dharma, they do not spare even their own bodies or lives;
seventh, regarding the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, as well as the purification of Buddha-fields, they cultivate the provisions of all merits without weariness.
Eighth, the perfect accomplishment of the majestic power of dhāraṇī;
ninth, the cultivation of the practice of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā because the mind is unstained by any mundane, worldly status;
tenth, the skillful means and wisdom that transcend and advance beyond all stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
“World-Honored One!
These are the ten kinds of definitive, unsurpassed bodhisattva practices that a practicing bodhisattva should study and cultivate.
These evil friends do not reveal wholesome matters to them, but instead create obstacles to the Path, saying to the bodhisattvas:”
"If you practice with diligent effort, you may attain Buddhahood; it cannot be attained through a mind of indolence.
If you do not achieve Bodhi for eight or even ten kalpas, there will be no further possibility of seeking Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"World-Honored One!

When a bodhisattva practicing asceticism and diligence is obstructed by another from the path and caused to regress into the stage of the śrāvaka fruit, this is the tenth obstacle for a practicing bodhisattva—the demon’s hook of non-virtuous friends."

"Furthermore, World-Honored One, if a practicing bodhisattva is arrogant and conceited, because of that arrogance and because his mind does not humble itself, he will have no sense of submissiveness toward his teachers, preceptors, the monastic community, the ritual procedures (*karmavācanā*), his disciples, donors, and even his parents."

If one sees a bodhisattva who has already transcended the gates of bodhisattva practice, attained mastery in virtuous conduct, and acquired dhāraṇīs with perfect deportment, yet does not wish to draw near them, does not train together with them, and does not seek out or inquire after their excellent instructions; [this is a fault].

If one sees a practitioner who has previously cultivated the Mahāyāna, their mind having already been hooked by the hook of Māra, for this reason that person instead cultivates perverse practices, delights in evil companions, and exclusively follows wrong paths; they fall away from Bodhi, like a foolish ewe who makes no forward progress.

It is, for example, like a person during a time of drought who plants a jambu tree on the high plains and dry land, yet fails to irrigate it, even though there are flowing canals whose embankments have been blocked and severed.
"World-Honored One, although this person has planted [the seed], it will not grow because they do not irrigate it.

It is the same for a bodhisattva who practices: having first resolved upon bodhicitta, they later give rise to arrogance and conceit; consequently, they fall away from the instructions of their spiritual friends and do not hear the Buddha-dharma."
Having already heard and received [the teaching], one no longer needs to cultivate or refine it.

It is like the water of the ocean, where the waves do not stir; because the terrain is low-lying, the water becomes deep and vast, and all rivers, streams, and springs flow together toward that lower ground.
World-Honored One!

It is the same for a bodhisattva who practices the path: toward their preceptors, teachers, and parents, they maintain a humble mind; by expending little effort, they obtain the great and profound Dharma, and as soon as it is brought to mind, the Dharma enters their heart.
If one is arrogant and conceited, and does not submit to teachers, monks, or parents, you should know that this person has already been caught by the hook of Māra.
World-Honored One!
This is the eleventh obstacle for a practicing bodhisattva—the demon’s hook of arrogance.

Furthermore, World-Honored One, if a practicing bodhisattva possesses a dignified and handsome appearance that is revered by all; if he is wealthy and of noble lineage, with a vast retinue, dependents, storehouses, and precious treasures in immeasurable number; yet...
Because of his dignified appearance, he is admired by all;
being wealthy and of noble lineage, with a large retinue and a vast accumulation of merit, he is held in high esteem and venerated.

Yet this bodhisattva does not seek to accumulate the provisions for knowledge; due to the power of his own majesty and wealth, his mind becomes intoxicated and arrogant, and he fails to see the correct path.

If one sees a renunciant who has newly undertaken the Bodhisattva precepts, having emerged from the toils of worldly existence, diligently practicing and accumulating the provisions of wisdom; by the power of such wisdom, they sit in meditation with sincere devotion for the sake of the Dharma amidst wind and sun until their flesh and blood are parched and their bones are emaciated, practicing morning and evening as if their hair were on fire.

If a bodhisattva who practices with arrogance sees such a practitioner and conceives feelings of disdain or contempt, refusing to associate with them or follow their instructions, his mind is deluded, dull-witted, and devoid of wisdom.
“World-Honored One!
This is the twelfth obstacle for a practicing bodhisattva—the demon’s hook that intoxicates with the mind of self.
At that time, the bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
These are the twelve kinds of *aṅkuśā* (hooks) of demonic obstacles for practicing bodhisattvas, which cause hindrances to the path for those practicing as bodhisattvas.

If a practicing bodhisattva does not perceive, does not know, does not depart from, and does not distance themselves from such ignorance, they are not yet even fit to practice the conduct of a novice bodhisattva; how much less could they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?”
Therefore, a bodhisattva who is first practicing should diligently collect the mind and personally realize that they have transcended the twelve hooks of demonic obstacles.

This is the thirteenth [chapter], extracted from the *Līlāvyūha-sūtra*, which clearly explains a single path of practice: through skillful means, one provides the pleasures of the five desires to convert all sentient beings, causing them to resolve upon unsurpassed bodhi.
At that time, the Elder Subhūti addressed the lady, saying:
"Noble woman! Where is your husband now?"
The lady replied: "Subhūti,
you should know that I do not have only one husband now."
"Why is this? Because all the sentient beings of the world, being entangled by the five desires and habituated to playful pleasures, are all my husbands. Subhūti said:
“What is skillful means for playing at will? The lady replied,
“Subhūti, you should know this:”

If there are sentient beings who greedily crave the five desires, I shall provide them with the necessary resources and offerings, thereby exhorting and transforming them so that they may resolve to attain Bodhi.

If there are sentient beings whose lustful minds are burning intensely, I shall redirect my gifts to allow them to indulge in their pleasures as they wish; for this reason, it is called "skillful means of playful enjoyment according to one's will."
Subhūti said: "The Tathāgata does not permit sentient beings to indulge in desire. The lady replied:
"As it is stated in the sūtras spoken by the Tathāgata:

'If there is a bhikṣu who receives and maintains the saffron robe, the mendicant’s staff, bedding, medicinal requisites for illness, and various articles of personal use, he should not store them in excess.'"

Whatever excellent and sublime offerings these youths and various donors obtain within the village, they shall offer them to the teachers, the preceptors, and the resident monks, who may accept them as they see fit; if, by means of even a single such object, their evil conduct is extinguished and they attain the long path [of liberation].
"For this reason, the Tathāgata has permitted those bhikṣus to accept and keep these items.
Subhūti said: "It is exactly as you have said; it is true and not false."
The lady said: "Regarding all the five desires and the attachment to playful pleasures, the Tathāgata, through these skillful means, permits them without prohibition if there is some benefit."
Subhūti said: "O daughter of good family!
How many sentient beings, by means of these skillful means, experience various playful delights and mature for unsurpassed bodhi?"
The lady replied:
"If one were to reach the very limit of the number of stars existing within the space of the trichiliocosm, one might still know their total count."

If, through my skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), they are tamed, exhorted, and transformed by the enjoyment of worldly play, and thereby all give rise to the aspiration for unexcelled bodhi—such sentient beings would be more numerous than the stars in the sky.
Subhūti said: "O virtuous woman!
How are you able to cause all sentient beings to obtain peace and happiness?"
The lady replied:

"Subhūti, you should know that there are sentient beings who delight in the affairs of the Brahma-heaven; I provide them with the joy and bliss of the four dhyānas according to their wishes, and thereafter exhort them to resolve upon bodhicitta."
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who delight in serving Śakra; I shall provide them with the pleasures of Śakra and then exhort them to resolve upon bodhicitta.

Furthermore, there are sentient beings who delight in the play and amusements of the various devas, nāga kings, yakṣas, asuras, gandharvas, garuḍas, and diverse great serpents; I shall provide each with whatever they enjoy without fail, and then exhort them to resolve upon bodhicitta.

Furthermore, there are sentient beings whose inclinations are for the playful enjoyments of a universal wheel-turning monarch, or even for those of high ministers, city-dwellers, village folk, sons of noble families, and brahmins of middle or low status; for such beings, he bestows everything according to their respective inclinations so that none may lack anything, and only thereafter exhorts them to resolve upon bodhicitta.

Furthermore, there are sentient beings who delight in forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects; there are sentient beings whose minds are greedily attached to flower garlands, necklaces, ointments, powdered incense, clothing, and silken fabrics as ornaments; and there are sentient beings who are greedily attached to wealth, gold, silver, pearls, jade, crystal, agate, drums, music, and song. For all such sentient beings, whatever they delight in—the playful pleasures of the five desires—one should provide them with these, and thereafter exhort them to resolve upon Bodhicitta.
Subhūti said: "Good women should know this:
these five desires obstruct the Eightfold Noble Path; they prevent one from attaining the wholesome state on the path leading to Nirvāṇa."

When these beings are fully immersed in the five desires, there are also sentient beings who, by virtue of this very condition, are exhorted toward the well-disciplined state of entering into bodhi; the sequence of this meaning is exceedingly difficult to conceive.
"O virtuous woman!
You should know that it is exceedingly difficult for a great bodhisattva to cause this practicing bodhisattva to accomplish wholesome deeds through the performance of such extremely arduous tasks."

Why is this? Such matters as these are all of one kind—obstacles to the Path for sentient beings; yet there are also various classes of sentient beings who, conversely, enter into goodness by means of being tamed.

At that time, in the midst of the Dharma assembly at the vihāra, there were two sons of elders who had previously been intimate with the lady; because they had skillfully employed means to provide her with playful enjoyment according to her wishes, they exhorted her to enter unsurpassed bodhi.
At that time, these two sons of a householder addressed Subhūti, saying:
"Subhūti! Do not use your own wisdom to discriminate against the wisdom of others."
Subhūti, what do you think?
If there were a small amount of oil lamp, could it be extinguished by blowing on it with the mouth or fanning it with the hand?
Subhūti said, “It would be easily blown out.
The son of the householder said:

"In the same way, if a son or daughter of good family who practices as a śrāvaka, by means of a small degree of the light of wisdom and through a single playful wisdom, is able to extinguish it, it is likewise so."
Subhūti, you should know this:

for example, at the end of a kalpa, seven suns appear, and by the light of these many suns, great flames arise throughout the world. Would it be possible to extinguish such a fire with the waters of the Ganges River?
Subhūti said: "Even the waters of a hundred thousand oceans could not extinguish it; how much less could the waters of the Ganges?
The son of the householder said:
“Subhūti, you should know this:

regarding such immeasurable and boundless radiance of wisdom and immeasurable and boundless radiance of merit of a bodhisattva—if a practicing bodhisattva were to indulge in the play and entertainment of the five desires and experience worldly pleasures for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, no one would be able to withstand or extinguish the radiance of that practicing bodhisattva’s wisdom and the radiance of his merit.”
For example, suppose there is a poor and sick person who seeks medical treatment for his illness; because of his poverty, the physician prescribes a simple remedy.
At that time, the poor person, wishing for his illness to be cured, takes the medicine which is inexpensive in price, and his illness is eliminated.
Why is this? It is because that poor and sick person lacks strength.

The śrāvaka is likewise: by practicing the twelve dhūtas to restrain the mind, dwelling alone in an araṇya, and delighting in coarse and worn-out robes, he subsequently attains liberation from worldly afflictions.
Subhūti, you should know this:
just as a poor and sick person is given medicine by a skilled physician according to their specific condition with the wish for the illness to be cured, so too is the liberation of the śrāvaka.

"Furthermore, it is like this: suppose there is a Kṣatriya king who has received the consecration. If the king falls ill, a skilled physician prepares for him a noble medicine that is lustrous and fragrant, sweet to the lips and mouth, brings peace to the four limbs, and is fit for the king to take.
Once the king had taken the medicine, he was presented with music, flowers, incense, and entertainments to provide him with pleasure; by these skillful means, the king’s illness was cured.
Subhūti, you should know that it is likewise so:

there are also practicing bodhisattvas who, through skillful means, enjoy the five desires as they please for the sake of playful delight, and by means of this joyful vehicle, they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Subhūti, you should know this:
just as a king who is ill takes the most excellent and sublime medicine, so too is it for a bodhisattva in practice; by the power of skillful means and wisdom, they attain liberation.

Chapter Fourteen: From the *Sūtra on Skillful Means*, explaining one type of practice that serves as the cause for committing a grave obstruction when practicing the bodhisattva path while performing the practices of a śrāvaka.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Anuttara-jñāna, saying: "Good son!
If there is a bhikṣu who practices the bodhisattva path and commits various grave offenses, he can eliminate them through skillful means."
"For this reason, I shall now explain for you the causes and conditions by which there is no offense.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Anuttaraprajñā addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
“How does a practicing bodhisattva commit an offense?
The Buddha said, “Good son!

If a practicing bodhisattva cultivates the practices of the śrāvakas—even if for hundreds of thousands of kalpas they consume the roots, stalks, flowers, and fruits of medicinal herbs, and are able to endure the good and evil words and breath of all sentient beings—because they have cultivated meditative concentration within the practices of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, this constitutes a grave transgression for a practicing bodhisattva.
"Good son! For example, once a śrāvaka has committed the four grave offenses, these five aggregates in their present body can no longer serve as a vessel for attaining nirvāṇa. Good son!"

It is likewise so: if a practicing bodhisattva does not abandon the śrāvakas and does not repent their transgressions, that practicing bodhisattva will no longer be capable of attaining equal and perfect enlightenment, nor will they be able to enter the Buddha-ground of nirvana without remainder.
Fifteenth, Fifteenth: From the *Sāgaramati-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, explaining one path of practice; it describes how a practicing bodhisattva may regress and enter into the practice of a śrāvaka.
"Furthermore, good son!
It is like a person suffering from an eye ailment who, after a month has passed, undergoes medical treatment with medicine, and his eyes gradually open and see.
