The power of this vehicle is to cause all sentient beings to enter it, to accumulate the provisions of merit and roots of goodness, to purify and embrace the various *pāramitās* for the sake of all beings, and to cause them to enter into all dharmas; thus, one constantly practices the Buddha-way without interruption.
Because this vehicle is unimpeded, it is illuminated by radiance.
If one enters this Mahāyāna, all sentient beings become mendicants, transcending all fear-inducing wrong paths.
In this vehicle, the sublime virtues of the Tathāgata are ever present before one’s eyes; it is capable of subduing all demons, heterodox paths, and miscellaneous practices.
Furthermore, it serves as the Tathāgata’s support for virtuous conduct, like a jeweled banner upon a tree that stands without interruption.

This vehicle can eliminate dwelling within the three realms and extinguish the deluded imaginings of the two extremes; it can sever and eradicate all doubts held by the fetters of impermanence and the grasping at the sign of emptiness, because the Tathāgata’s Buddha-vehicle is attained without obstruction.

This vehicle is able to approach the Three Jewels within the collection of all dharmas and benefit the people of the world; all should rely upon it as their refuge. It traverses the path of non-deception because all sentient beings possess a share in it, and because of the power of the firm persistence of past great compassion, it manifests at this place.

By means of the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the eighteen unique qualities, the thirty-two marks, and the eighty minor characteristics—adorned with the radiance of the ornaments of body, speech, and mind—one becomes free from reproach and fault in all circumstances; this is the skillful means practiced within the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva.

The thirty-eighth [chapter], from the *Ugraparipṛcchā-sūtra*, clearly explains one method of practice: it teaches that a lay bodhisattva should cultivate four kinds of practices as the reasons for not renouncing the household life.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the householder Ugga, saying:
"A bodhisattva practicing as a layperson attains refuge in the Tathāgata by means of four kinds of practices."
What are the four? They are:
first, because the bodhicitta is never abandoned;...
Second, not breaking the practice of samādhi and dhyāna;
third, because great loving-kindness and great compassion are uninterrupted;
fourth, not being defiled by or mixing with other vehicles.
These are the four kinds of practice through which one achieves refuge in the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of karmic activities through which one attains refuge in the Dharma. What are these four?
That is to say:
first, making offerings to the Dharma teacher;
second, listening to the Dharma with reverence.
Third, having heard the Dharma, one seeks it out with upright integrity;
fourth, having heard the essentials of the Dharma, one explains them for the sake of sentient beings, circulating and dedicating them so that all may attain equal and perfect enlightenment.
"Furthermore, there are four kinds of practices through which one attains refuge in the Sangha.
What are these four? They are as follows:"
First, not delighting in the vehicle of the śrāvakas, but exclusively seeking unsurpassed bodhi;
second, if there are sentient beings practicing other types of deeds, exhorting them to practice and study the true and correct Buddha-dharma;
third, never retreating from the bodhicitta.
Fourth, they make offerings to the monastic community, investigating the practices of the śrāvakas while not adopting their liberation.
When practicing the bodhisattva path, having relinquished all material wealth, they give rise to a mind of giving with wisdom, thinking:
"If there are those who come in hunger to beg for food and drink, I shall give them all, even if it be alcohol."
He further reflects: "All that is sought shall bring about the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā).
In this way, the lay-practicing bodhisattva maintains and protects the practice of ethical discipline (śīla).
At that time, the Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Did you see how the householder Ugga made offerings to the Tathāgata, cultivated the Dharma, and was able to give away whatever things he delighted in?"
Ānanda said to the Buddha,
“World-Honored One!
I have seen this matter.”
The Buddha said:
“Ānanda, you should know this:

throughout this Bhadrakalpa, all one thousand Buddhas who appear in the world shall be universally honored by the householder Ugga with immeasurable offerings. He will uphold and protect the Buddha-dharma; though he remains in lay attire, he cultivates the conduct of a monk and extensively practices the path of the Buddha.”
At that time, Ānanda asked the householder Ugga: "Householder!
For what reason—though the secular life is like a hostile thief—do you dwell happily in the garments and state of a layperson?"
"Now that you have encountered the conditions for leaving the household life,
why do you lack a joyful heart? The elder replied,
"I do not delight in the secular world."

Why is this? Because a practicing bodhisattva is endowed with great compassion; they do not seek personal pleasure, endure suffering and affliction for the sake of others, and never abandon sentient beings.
The Buddha said, “Ānanda!
You should know that although this householder Ugga is dressed in the garb of a layperson, he has already brought immeasurable sentient beings to spiritual maturity.”
None of the other hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas were able to mature sentient beings in such a manner. Why is this?
Because those hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas all lacked such skillful means and majestic power as that of the householder Ugga alone.

The thirty-ninth [chapter], the thirty-ninth from the *Suviśuddha-śīla-sūtra*, elucidates two modes of practice: First, the initiation of practice whereby a bodhisattva is worthy of receiving immeasurable offerings of clothing, food, bedding, and seats, and the merit thereof is immeasurable.
Furthermore, this also manifests the supernatural power of the Naga King Anavatapta.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the sons of good family, saying:
"O sons of good family!..."
One should engage in battle with Māra and seek the state of the Noble Ones.

When a Bodhisattva practices to bring sentient beings to maturity, he first battles with malevolent demons to transform them, acting in accordance with wholesome conduct and seeking no other teacher; this is called the practice of the Dharma.
"Sons of good family, you should know this:
if there are those who disparage the practitioners of the śrāvaka path, you should not disparage them;
if there are those who delight in cultivating the śrāvaka path, you should not delight in it."
At that time, the bodhisattvas addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is it that constitutes the conduct censured by śrāvakas yet not censured by bodhisattvas, and what is it that śrāvakas seek while bodhisattvas do not seek?”
The Buddha said:
"If the śrāvakas revile and loathe birth and death, you should not loathe them;
if the śrāvakas aspire to and delight in nirvāṇa, you should not aspire to or delight in it—this is the practice of the Dharma."
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying: “Śāriputra!
Suppose there were great bodhisattvas practicing the path, filling the world, who daily bestowed robes and garments upon all sentient beings.”
"What do you think?

Such giving is a gift of supreme purity; it is not only for the sake of the initial aspiration for unsurpassed bodhicitta of a beginner Bodhisattva, but from that point onward, it becomes most excellent, such that the practicing Bodhisattva is worthy of receiving such a gift of clothing."

If a bodhisattva who has first begun their practice were to receive pure meat offerings from others daily, accumulating as much as Mount Sumeru, they would still be able to accept them purely; yet this is not because the bodhisattva practicing for the first time has generated the unsurpassed bodhicitta. From that point onward, however, they become supreme, and as a practicing bodhisattva, they are capable of receiving such pure food.

If a bodhisattva who has first begun their practice should enjoy a high seat as vast as the four continents, as high as Mount Sumeru, composed of the seven treasures—gold, silver, crystal, pearl, agate, diamond, and various other gems—inlaid and adorned with them, and covered above by the fine garments of the devas.

That seat is purified through the pure enjoyment of all sentient beings each day; it is not for the sake of the initial resolve of a beginner bodhisattva who has first generated the mind of unsurpassed enlightenment. From this point forward, one shall become a donor for all sentient beings and is thus worthy of receiving such a high seat.
“Śāriputra, you should know:
it is like the four great rivers that emerge from the four sides of the palace of the Naga King Anavatapta. What are these four?
They are: first, the Ganges; second, the Sindhu; third, the Vakṣu; and fourth, the Sītā.
These four great rivers flow into the great ocean, causing it to be filled to overflowing.
Each of these four great rivers has its own retinue:
the river Gaṅgā has five hundred small rivers as its retinue and flows into the great ocean in the east;
the river Sītā has five hundred small rivers as its retinue and flows into the great ocean in the south.
If the great river Vakṣu has five hundred small rivers as its tributaries, it flows westward into the great ocean;
if the great river Sindhu has five hundred small rivers as its tributaries, it flows northward into the great ocean.
Śāriputra, what do you think?
Do these four rivers flow out according to their respective directions to fill the four great oceans, flowing everywhere through the wilderness to benefit the sentient beings of the world?
Śāriputra said: “World-Honored One!
These four great rivers benefit immeasurable sentient beings, humans, non-humans, and others.”

“In this way, the great and small rivers flow into the world, moistening the five grains—rice, mung beans, various wheat, sesame, and cotton fields—and all such diverse fields are irrigated by these rivers.”
Śāriputra, what do you think?
How could these four great oceans ever be filled?
Śāriputra said, “It is because of these four great rivers that it becomes full.
The Buddha said:
"Śāriputra, what do you think?
How many sentient beings can these four great rivers benefit within the great ocean?"
Śāriputra said: “World-Honored One! You benefit immeasurable sentient beings;

you provide the foremost benefit to sentient beings of water and land—fish, turtles, soft-shelled turtles, crocodiles, sharks, makaras, pythons, snakes, and myriad other species; sea-folk, oysters, clams, and conch insects; all dragon mothers and their offspring; asuras, rākṣasas, humans, and non-humans—you are able to benefit them all.”

Various kinds of miscellaneous jewels fill the ocean; oysters, clams, and pearls emit light that shakes the earth. Crystal, agate, musaragalva, conch shell, amber, karketana, coral, and various other treasures fill the ocean, bringing benefit to sentient beings.
“Śāriputra! What do you think? From what do these four great oceans arise?”
Śāriputra said: "It exists because of the dragon king Anavatapta.
The Buddha said:
“Śāriputra! This Dragon King Anavatapta does not encounter three difficulties.
What are these three difficulties?
First, they do not fear being swallowed by the garuḍa;
second, hot sand does not fall upon their bodies;
third, when engaging in sexual desire, they do not transform into snakes.
All other dragon kings encounter three hardships, but the Dragon King Anavatapta alone is free from these difficulties.

The palace of the Dragon King Anavatapta is constantly inhabited by those who dwell in supernormal powers and meditative concentration; for all sentient beings who enter his palace, the hot sand does not fall upon their bodies.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the World-Honored One, saying: “World-Honored One,
how does the palace of the Dragon King Anavatapta come to possess such wondrous merit, virtue, and majestic power?”

For what reason do all other dragon kings encounter calamities during the six periods of day and night, while this Dragon King Anavatapta and his palace alone are free from such hardships, and instead possess immeasurable roots of goodness and merit that flow forth as the four rivers to benefit the livelihoods of immeasurable sentient beings?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"It is exactly as you have said; the Dragon King Anavatapta is a great bodhisattva, a bodhisattva of great cultivation."
Śāriputra! Just as the Naga King Anavatapta attains liberation from three kinds of hardships,
so too does the practicing bodhisattva likewise attain liberation from the three kinds of calamities.
What are these three?
They are the hardship of the hells, the hardship of the hungry ghosts, and the hardship of the animals.
It is like the four rivers from the pool of the Dragon King Anavatapta, which secretly moisten and extensively pervade the fields and plains.
The practice of a bodhisattva is likewise thus: they gather all sentient beings through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).
What are these four? First, gathering through generosity (*dāna*); [and so forth].
Second is the means of attraction through kind speech;
third is the means of attraction through beneficial conduct;
fourth is the means of attraction through cooperation.

Śāriputra! Just as the waters of the four great oceans are brought to fulfillment by the four great rivers of the Naga King Anavatapta, so too is it with a bodhisattva who has first begun their practice:
through the generation of the bodhicitta, they bring about unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).
For example, it is like the immeasurable, boundless, and countless hundreds of thousands of millions of sentient beings who experience happiness within the four great oceans.

Śāriputra, you should know that the establishment of sentient beings within the three realms within the Buddha-dharma is likewise so; one should see that the sentient beings of the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm, as well as the sentient beings of the trichiliocosm who receive such happiness, all do so because of the merit manifested through the response-appearances of bodhisattvas.

Forty-fourth: Extracted from the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*, this reveals the practice of a single path—the practice of the bodhisattva cultivating the six pāramitās while abiding in the stages (*bhūmi*).
At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How many kinds of training are there for these practicing bodhisattvas, which bodhisattvas dwelling on the stages (*bhūmi*) should study so as to be able to achieve unsurpassed bodhi?”
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, saying:
“Good son, you should know that there are briefly six kinds of stages for dwelling in the training of a bodhisattva.”
What are these six? They are:
generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Of these six kinds of training and abiding stages, how many are subsumed under the training in ethical discipline?"
"How many are subsumed under the training in concentration?
How many are subsumed under the training in wisdom?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, saying:

“Good son! You should know that among the first three types of training—namely, generosity, ethical discipline, and patience—these three should be understood as being subsumed within the training in ethical discipline (śīla-śikṣā).
As for the single type of meditative concentration (dhyāna), it is subsumed solely within the training in higher mind (adhicitta-śikṣā).”
"If it is wisdom, it is subsumed under the training in higher wisdom;
if it is diligence, I say it pervades all.
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Among these six stages of training, how many are comprised within the accumulation of merit,
and how many are comprised within the accumulation of wisdom?”
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, saying:
"Good son! If it is subsumed by the training in ethical discipline, it is called being subsumed by the provision of merit."
If it is subsumed under the cultivation and study of wisdom, it is called being subsumed under the accumulation of wisdom;
I say that diligence and meditative concentration pervade all, and thus they also enter into the accumulation of merit as well as being subsumed under the accumulation of wisdom.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Regarding these six kinds of training:
First, at the outset, one firmly establishes the practice and vows regarding the subtle and sublime True Dharma associated with the *pāramitās* of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka;
second, subsequently, one diligently practices the ten types of Dharma-activities through the wisdom accomplished by hearing, reflection, and cultivation;
third, one protects and upholds the bodhicitta.
"Fourth, one should draw near to and make offerings to true spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), and cultivate wholesome qualities (kuśaladharma) with uninterrupted diligence.
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva said:
"World-Honored One!"
"For what reason are these six stages of training?
I wish to know the cause for each of these six numbers.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, saying:
“Good son! It is due to two causes and conditions:
first, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings;”
Second, because they serve as antidotes to all afflictions. Avalokiteśvara,
you should know that among these six trainings, the first three benefit sentient beings:
Generosity, ethical discipline, and patience;
the latter three counteract all causes of affliction:
diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
Among these, the bodhisattva practicing with the first three types [of giving] gathers in and sustains sentient beings through various material requisites by means of generosity;
and by means of ethical discipline, they refrain from harming, oppressing, or harassing them, thereby causing them to be free from enemies.
Because of patience, when others come to harm, oppress, or afflict one, one is able to endure them and protect sentient beings.
Avalokiteśvara! You should know that these three which have been explained are the causes for the giving of protection to sentient beings.

Regarding the three subsequent types of remedies for the afflictions (*kleśa*): through the cultivation of diligence (*vīrya*), the bodhisattva causes the afflictions to be shaken and, by means of training, is able to counteract them while courageously cultivating all categories of wholesome qualities;
through the training in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one is able to strip away the afflictions from the mind;
and through wisdom (*prajñā*), the afflictions are eradicated forever.
These latter three types serve as the remedies for the causes of affliction.

[Section] Forty-one: From the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-ekayāna-mahā-upāya-vaipulya-sūtra*, the exposition of a single path of practice, the manifestation of the Tathāgata through the proclamation of ten great vows and aspirations. When one praises the Tathāgata, the Tathāgata then appears.
At that time, King Prasenajit and Queen Mallikā, having recently placed their faith in the Dharma, said to one another:
"Lady Śrīmālā is our daughter; she is wise, of sharp faculties, and possesses quick intelligence and ease of understanding."
"If one beholds the Buddha, one will surely and swiftly understand the Dharma, and the mind will attain freedom from doubt.
It is fitting that you dispatch a messenger at this time to inspire the aspiration for the Way. The lady said:
"Now is precisely the right time.

The King and the Queen Consort wrote a letter to Śrīmālā, briefly extolling the immeasurable merits of the Tathāgata. They then dispatched an attendant woman named Caṇḍilā as a messenger to deliver the letter to the kingdom of Ayodhyā; she entered the palace and respectfully presented it to Śrīmālā.
Having received the letter, Śrīmālā received it with joy upon the crown of her head; she read, recited, and upheld it, giving rise to a sense of rare wonder, and spoke these verses toward Caṇḍila:
"I have heard the voice of the Buddha, Unprecedented in this world.
That which he has spoken is true; One ought to practice offerings to it."
I look up with reverence to the Buddha, the World-Honored One, who has appeared for the sake of all in the world;
may you also deign to show compassion, and I pray that you will surely grant me a vision.
As soon as this thought arose, the Buddha manifested in the midst of the sky.
Universally emitting pure radiance, he revealed his incomparable body.
Vaśitā and her retinue bowed their heads to his feet in prostration;
with hearts of pure clarity, they praised the Buddha’s true merits:
“The Tathāgata’s wondrous form-body is peerless in the world;
it is incomparable and inconceivable—therefore, I now pay homage.
The Tathāgata’s form is inexhaustible, and his wisdom is likewise.”
All phenomena are eternally abiding; therefore, I take refuge.
Having subdued the faults of the mind and the four kinds of bodily [faults], you have reached the stage that is difficult to subdue; therefore, I pay homage to the Dharma King.
Just as all things are suchness, you possess mastery over the body of wisdom and sustain all phenomena; therefore, I now pay homage to you.
Homage to you who transcend all measure; homage to you who are beyond comparison.
Homage to the boundless Dharma; homage to the inconceivable.
May you take pity on me and protect me, causing the seeds of the Dharma to grow.
In this life and in future births, may the Buddha always sustain me with his grace.
"I have long established you in peace; you were already awakened in previous lives.
Now I again receive you, and it shall be so in future births as well.
I have performed meritorious deeds in the present and in other worlds."
"May these roots of all such virtues be graciously accepted by you.
At that time, having heard her prediction, Lady Śrīmālā stood with reverence and undertook the ten great vows, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"From this day forth until I attain enlightenment, I shall not give rise to a mind of transgression regarding the precepts I have received.
World-Honored One!
From this day forth until I attain enlightenment, I shall not give rise to a mind of pride toward my elders and superiors."
“World-Honored One!
From this day forth until I attain enlightenment, I shall not give rise to a mind of anger toward any sentient being.
World-Honored One!”
"From this day forth until I attain enlightenment, I shall not give rise to envy toward the physical forms of others or their external requisites.
World-Honored One!
From this day forth until I attain enlightenment, I shall not give rise to avarice regarding internal or external phenomena."
“World-Honored One!

From this day forth until I attain enlightenment, I shall not accept or store wealth and goods for my own sake; whatever I do receive, I shall do entirely for the purpose of bringing poverty-stricken sentient beings to maturity.”
“World-Honored One!

From this day forth until I attain bodhi, I shall not practice the four methods of attraction for my own sake; rather, for the sake of all sentient beings, I shall gather in and sustain them with a mind free from attachment, a mind free from weariness, and an unobstructed mind.”
“World-Honored One!

From this day forth until I attain enlightenment, if I see sentient beings who are solitary, imprisoned, ill, or afflicted by various calamities and hardships, I shall never abandon them for even a moment. I must bring them peace and security, benefit them through righteous means, and cause them to be liberated from all suffering before I finally depart.”
“World-Honored One!

From this day forth until I attain enlightenment, if I see those who capture and raise animals—those of evil discipline—or those who violate the precepts, I shall never abandon them. When I have attained power, wherever I may see such sentient beings, I shall subdue those who should be subdued and embrace those who should be embraced.”
Why is this? Because through subduing and gathering [disciples], the Dharma is made to endure for a long time.
When the Dharma endures for a long time, devas and humans flourish, the evil realms diminish, and one is able to follow and turn the wheel of Dharma turned by the Tathāgata.
Seeing this benefit, he rescues and gathers [beings] without abandoning them.
"World-Honored One!
From this day forth until I attain Bodhi, I shall uphold the True Dharma and never forget it."

Why is this? One who forgets the Dharma forgets the Mahāyāna; one who forgets the Mahāyāna forgets the pāramitās; one who forgets the pāramitās does not desire the Mahāyāna Bodhisattva path; and one who is not resolved upon the Mahāyāna cannot embrace the aspiration for the True Dharma or enter it according to their inclination, being forever incapable of transcending the stage of ordinary beings.

Having seen such immeasurable great faults, and furthermore having seen the immeasurable benefits for the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who will receive and uphold the True Dharma in the future, I accept this great undertaking.
“Lord of Dharma, World-Honored One!
May You now bear witness for me; it is only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, who can directly perceive and know this.

Yet, because the roots of goodness in sentient beings are feeble, they may fall into the net of doubt—since the ten great vows are extremely difficult to fulfill—they might, for a long night, fail to obtain benefit, meaning, or peace and happiness. For their sake, I now speak this vow of truth before the Buddha.”

As I have received these ten great vows and shall practice them as prescribed, by virtue of this oath, may celestial flowers rain down and celestial, wondrous sounds emerge within this great assembly.
When these words were spoken, a rain of various celestial flowers fell from the void, and a wondrous voice proclaimed:
"So it is, so it is! It is exactly as you have said; it is true and not otherwise."
Upon seeing those flowers and hearing those sounds, all the members of the assembly were completely freed from their doubts and perplexities; leaping with immeasurable joy, they made this vow:
"May we always be together with Śrīmālā and may our practices be identical to hers."
The World-Honored One bestowed upon the entire great assembly the fulfillment of their respective aspirations.
At that time, Queen Śrīmālā again made three great vows before the Buddha, speaking these words:

"By means of this sincere vow, may I bring comfort to immeasurable and boundless sentient beings; by means of these roots of goodness, may I attain the wisdom of the True Dharma in every birth—this is called the first great vow."
Having attained the wisdom of the True Dharma, I shall preach it for the sake of sentient beings with an insatiable mind; this is called the second great vow.
Regarding the upholding of the True Dharma, I shall sacrifice my body, life, and wealth to protect and maintain it; this is called the third great vow.
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately confirmed Śrīmālā’s three great vows:

"Just as all forms are entirely contained within the realm of space, so too do the river-sands of a bodhisattva's various vows all enter into these three great vows; these vows are truly vast and great."

Chapter Forty-two: The Manifest Explanation of the Threefold Practice from the *Sūtra of the Dhāraṇī of the Gate of Boundless Birth*. It is taught that when one who upholds this sūtra and its dhāraṇī approaches the end of life, eight billion Buddhas will personally come to welcome them.
Furthermore, it manifests the three bodies of the Tathāgata;
moreover, it explains that by practicing the four matters—the gate of signless practice—a bodhisattva swiftly attains the path to Buddhahood.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying:

*Sarvabuddha-tiṣṭhite nidhānagotre svāhā.* The Buddha said to Śāriputra:

"If a bodhisattva cultivates this dhāraṇī, they should not differentiate between the conditioned and the unconditioned; nor should they grasp or cling to them, nor increase or decrease them, nor establish or destroy them, nor conjoin or disperse them, nor produce or extinguish them. Furthermore, they should not dwell upon past, future, or present phenomena, nor should they accumulate or grasp at any phenomena. They should simply contemplate that the Buddhas are neither form nor formless, neither with marks nor without marks."
“A Bodhisattva should not, like those of the Two Vehicles, grasp at the Buddha’s form-body (rūpakāya). Why is this?

Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas grasp at the Buddha’s form-body as being characterized by marks of adornment and radiant illumination; they regard it as produced by parents and nurtured by food and drink, composed of blood, flesh, sinews, and bones, a synthesis of the four great elements, impermanent and subject to decay, suffering and impure—this they take to be the Buddha’s form-body.”
The Bodhisattva is not like this. Why?

Because the body of the Tathāgata is devoid of the characteristic of arising; for the sake of all sentient beings, he universally illuminates all phenomena through non-illumination, accumulating the provisions of wisdom to manifest the Dharma-body as having the characteristic of space and the characteristic of non-arising.

The Dharma-body of the Tathāgata takes the characteristic of non-arising as its aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), because the profound meaning of the characteristic of non-arising is the essence of all phenomena.
Nevertheless, bodhisattvas should not perceive the marks of the Tathāgata by means of what is not form.

If one perceives the marks of the Tathāgata by means of what is not form, one is the same as the śrāvakas—namely, those who claim that when the Buddha enters the nirvāṇa of extinction, his physical body is severed and extinguished, and will never again be reborn.
It is not so for the Bodhisattva. Why is this?

Because the body of the Tathāgata is characterized by inexhaustibility; for the sake of all sentient beings, he manifests a form-body through the illumination of non-illumination regarding all phenomena, and by taking dharmas as signs, he accumulates the provisions of merit.

Because the Tathāgata’s form-body possesses inexhaustible characteristics, this constitutes an inexhaustible aggregate of form; for this reason, all phenomena also possess inexhaustible characteristics.
As long as the realm of sentient beings has not been fully liberated, the Tathāgata constantly manifests an inexhaustible form-body.
“Śāriputra! Because of the dhāraṇīs within this sutra, immeasurable gateways of the face are produced.
If a practicing bodhisattva hears this sutra, they shall never regress from unsurpassed bodhi.”
Why is this? Because herein are revealed all the sublime virtues and supernormal powers of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, by means of this sutra, the ethical conduct of sentient beings is augmented, and they come to protect the dharma of non-apprehension through its gradual cultivation.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Do not take pleasure in or become attached to anything; all phenomena are empty.
Regarding the enlightenment of the Buddhas, do not give rise to conceptual discrimination."
Regarding bodhi and nirvāṇa, they likewise give rise to no doubt;
if one can practice this conduct, one will swiftly attain dhāraṇī.
By listening to this sūtra, one cultivates wisdom in emptiness and signlessness.
Neither arising nor ceasing, one shall swiftly realize bodhi.
The Bodhisattva who upholds this sutra deeply understands immeasurable dharmas;
they attain birth in the buddha-fields and draw near to the Most Victorious Honored One.
If one attains dhāraṇī, one will certainly comprehend the profound meaning and intent;
without giving rise to a mind of retreat or fear, one shall uphold the inexhaustible Dharma.
All the Buddhas of the ten directions, as they preach the Dharma, shall be heard in their entirety.
Having heard it, they shall all receive and uphold it, wearing it upon their heads and practicing it accordingly.
If one receives and upholds this sutra, regarding its words, phrases, and names,
as well as the sublime meaning therein, one shall never have doubt or forgetfulness.
Just as the light of the sun and moon Shines everywhere without exception,
So by understanding this Dharma-gate, One penetrates immeasurable meanings.
By reciting and upholding this sutra, One is able to achieve self-awakening and comprehension.
All supreme dharmas are the wondrous gateway of the *dhāraṇī*. Even if,
throughout the course of an eon, all sentient beings were to ask those who uphold this sūtra about every single one of their deep-seated doubts, [the upholder] would resolve them all.
At that time, the Bodhisattvas who uphold this sutra all expound it for others;
their nets of doubt are entirely removed, for the wisdom of Bodhisattvas is inexhaustible.
Because they cherish and delight in this sutra, they are able to swiftly draw near to Bodhi.
Such true children of the Buddha, Protect and uphold the secret treasury.
Holding this dhāraṇī, All sentient beings will revere and remember them;
All Buddhas together will praise them, And their fame shall reach throughout the ten directions.
By virtue of upholding this sutra, at the time when one is about to pass away,
one shall see eight billion buddhas extending their hands to receive and welcome [the practitioner],
all of whom speak these words:
"You shall go to my land.
By reciting and upholding this sutra, one receives such blessings in the present life.
Even if one has committed sins that would otherwise have to be endured for hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas, [they shall be extinguished].
By reciting this dhāraṇī, one becomes pure for an entire month.
Though a bodhisattva may diligently cultivate all merits throughout billions of kalpas,
if they recite this sūtra for a single month, their merit will surpass that of the former.
Through wholesome mindfulness, wisdom, and diligence, as well as samādhi and dhāraṇī,
these qualities will constantly manifest due to the power of this sutra, continuing until the stage of a Tathāgata.
Even if all sentient beings in the three realms were simultaneously to become Māras, [they could not obstruct it].
By reciting and upholding this sutra, none shall be able to create obstacles.
Within this sutra, all dharma-gates are explained;
therein the omniscience of all is taught, and by means of this, one attains perfect enlightenment.
Because I heard this sutra, Dīpaṃkara bestowed upon me a prophecy, saying:
"You shall attain Buddhahood and liberate all sentient beings."
At that time, they saw Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
hearing the Buddhas preach the Dharma, they were able to understand it all.
If they wish to receive and uphold the teachings spoken by all the Buddhas, [they shall do so].
By diligently practicing and studying this sutra, one will swiftly achieve such power.
The sublime adornment of buddha-fields, the great assemblies of holy beings,
their radiant marks, and their wondrous lineages— all are obtained from this sutra.
If a person, for seven days, Contemplates this sutra with focused attention, Eight billion Buddhas Will expound such a Dharma for them.
Be careful not to harbor wrong thoughts; Do not think what should not be thought.
With wisdom one should contemplate correctly, and swiftly attain this sutra.
Diligently practice this dharma-gate; do not fear that bodhi is far away.
It is like a person reaching a treasure island, gathering various jewels as they please.
If one upholds this dhāraṇī, do not say there is no karmic reward for goodness;
possessing the joys of humans and devas, it is not difficult to approach the Buddha-way.
If you wish to swiftly attain Buddhahood, you should uphold this sūtra.
"One will ultimately and certainly attain the unsurpassed, great Bodhi.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they will certainly and inevitably attain this dhāraṇī."
What are the four?
First, not delighting in sensual desires;
second, not giving rise to jealousy.
Third, they are able to relinquish everything for all sentient beings without any resentment or affliction;
fourth, they are joyful day and night, deeply delighting in seeking the Dharma. Śāriputra!
“A bodhisattva who accomplishes these four dharmas attains this dhāraṇī.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva accomplishes four other dharmas, they attain this dhāraṇī.”
What are the four? First, dwelling in the practice of a tranquil araṇya;
second, awakening to and entering into profound dharmakṣānti.
Third, not delighting in fame, reputation, or gain;
fourth, being able to relinquish all cherished things, even up to one's own body and life.
When a bodhisattva accomplishes these four dharmas, they attain this dhāraṇī.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they will obtain this dhāraṇī. What are these four?
This refers to entering into the meaning of the eight syllables.
What are the eight syllables?
"First is the syllable *pa*; it is the primary meaning (*paramārtha*), the meaning of entering into the selflessness of all phenomena."

"Second is the syllable LA: it enters the Tathāgata’s unborn Dharma-body; because it is not a collection of wisdom-merit through luminous illumination, it has no characteristic of entry; it takes the characteristic of non-arising as its form-body (rūpakāya) and takes the characteristic of inexhaustibility as the meaning of entering the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha)."
"Third, the letter Ma: the meaning of entering into the sameness of phenomena regarding wisdom and folly.
Fourth, the letter Ka: the meaning of entering into the non-existence of karmic retribution while discerning karmic retribution."
"Fifth is the syllable *Ja*: it awakens one to the meaning of entering into the non-arising and non-ceasing of birth, old age, sickness, and death.

Sixth is the syllable *Dha*: it awakens one to the fact that the essence of the *dhāraṇī* is empty, signless, and wishless, tranquil as *nirvāṇa*, thereby opening the understanding and entry into its meaning."

"Seventh, regarding the character *śamatha* (pronounced with a retroflex *ṣa*): it is the characteristic of dwelling in tranquil concentration (*śamatha*), while *vipaśyanā* is the correct vision of the characteristics of all phenomena (*dharmas*).
How does one dwell in tranquil concentration?..."

You should practice with diligent effort, day and night without interruption, contemplating the meditative image of the Buddha; you should not grasp at signs, but should instead maintain *vipaśyanā* and perceive correctly through wisdom.
If a practitioner sees a Buddha appear and considers it to be the true Buddha, they should reflect thus:
"From where does this Buddha whom I see come?
Does he come from the east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, or the zenith and nadir?"
If one considers this Buddha to be something created by a person, one should reflect:
"Is this Buddha made of clay or wood?
Or is it made of gold, silver, copper, or iron?"

Having observed in this way, he knows that the Buddha he sees appears only because he has been contemplating the image of the Buddha within the vihāra day and night; for this reason, the form of the Buddha constantly manifests before his eyes.
From this, one should know:

all phenomena that I have ever seen or heard and which I regard as real arise from the recollections of my own mind; this is precisely the first stage of cultivation for a bodhisattva, the meditative concentration of non-abiding, up to the stage of joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
"How does one contemplate the image of the Buddha while also abiding in the gateway of the ultimate truth?
One should form this thought:

'The image of the Buddha that I now see is not a characteristic belonging to the nature of the Buddha; it is only because I am currently observing the causes and conditions of the image that I see the form of the Buddha.'"
"Having entered into meditative concentration, one understands by analogy that all phenomena are likewise so.
For this reason, it should not be said that the physical forms of the Buddha are entirely non-existent."
One should know that the syllable *śa* is without distinction from all dharmas; they are all identical in their entry into the meaning of the Dharma-gate.
"Eighth, the syllable *kṣa*: all dharmas are empty, neither arising nor ceasing."
Why is this? Because one awakens to and understands that all phenomena are originally empty and quiescent, and that their self-nature is nirvana—this is the meaning of the entry [into the Dharma].
"One should uphold the meaning of these eight words in this manner; wherever there may be a copy of this sūtra, one should revere, honor, and make offerings to it."
Every half-month, one should recite and expound [this sūtra]; if one sees others studying and reciting this scripture, one should praise them and encourage their progress.
Śāriputra, if there are bodhisattvas who practice these four dharmas, they will attain this dhāraṇī.
Essential Collection from Various Sutras on the Gateways of Practice for Bodhisattvas in the Mahāyāna, Volume II.
